title: Chapter 29 — Enter Ahab; to Him, Stubb
paragraphs: Some days passed, and with ice and icebergs all astern, the Pequod now went rolling through the bright Quito spring — the endless spring of that city on the equator — which at sea reigns almost perpetually on the threshold of the eternal August of the Tropic. The warmly cool, clear, ringing, perfumed, overflowing, abundant days were like crystal goblets of Persian sherbet, heaped up — flaked up — with rose-water snow. The starry, stately nights seemed like haughty ladies in jeweled velvets, nursing at home in lonely pride the memory of their absent conquering Earls, the golden-helmeted suns! For a sleeping man, it was hard to choose between such winsome days and such seductive nights. But all the enchantments of that unfading weather did not merely lend new spells and powers to the outer world. They turned inward upon the soul, especially when the still, mild hours of evening came on; then memory shot out her crystals as clear ice forms most readily in noiseless twilights. And all these subtle influences worked more and more upon the fabric of Ahab.

Old age is always wakeful, as if the longer a man is linked with life, the less he has to do with anything that looks like death. Among sea captains, the old graybeards are the ones who most often leave their beds to visit the night-wrapped deck. So it was with Ahab, except that lately he seemed to live so much in the open air that, truly speaking, his visits were more to the cabin than from it. "It feels like going down into one's tomb," he would mutter to himself, "for an old captain like me to be descending this narrow hatch to my grave-dug bed."

So almost every twenty-four hours, when the night watches were set and the men on deck stood guard over the sleep of the men below; and when, if a rope had to be hauled on the forecastle, the sailors did not fling it down roughly, as by day, but dropped it carefully into its place for fear of disturbing their sleeping shipmates; when this sort of steady quiet would begin to settle in, the silent helmsman would habitually watch the cabin hatch; and before long the old man would emerge, gripping the iron railing to help his crippled way. There was some considerate touch of humanity in him; for at times like these he usually refrained from patrolling the quarter-deck, because to his weary mates, trying to rest within six inches of his ivory heel, the echoing crack and din of that bony step would have been such that their dreams would have been of the crunching teeth of sharks. But once, the mood was on him too deep for ordinary consideration; and as with a heavy, lumbering pace he was measuring the ship from the taffrail to the mainmast, Stubb, the old second mate, came up from below and, with a certain unsure, apologetic humor, hinted that if Captain Ahab was pleased to walk the planks, then no one could say no; but there might be some way of muffling the noise — hinting something vaguely and hesitantly about a ball of tow, and inserting the ivory heel into it. Ah, Stubb, you did not know Ahab then.

"Am I a cannonball, Stubb," said Ahab, "that you'd wad me like that? But go your way — I forgot. Down to your nightly grave, where the likes of you sleep wrapped in shrouds, getting used to the one you'll fill at last. Down, dog, and to your kennel!"

Startled by the unforeseen closing exclamation of the so suddenly scornful old man, Stubb was speechless for a moment; then said excitedly, "I'm not used to being spoken to that way, sir; I like it less than half, sir."
"Enough!" Ahab growled through clenched teeth, moving violently away as if to avoid some passionate temptation.
"No, sir, not yet," said Stubb, growing bolder. "I won't meekly accept being called a dog, sir."
"Then be called ten times a donkey, and a mule, and an ass, and get out of my sight, or I'll rid the world of you!"
As he said this, Ahab advanced on him with such overpowering menace in his bearing that Stubb involuntarily backed away.

"I was never served like that before without giving a hard blow for it," muttered Stubb, as he found himself going down the cabin hatch. "It's very queer. Stop, Stubb; somehow, now, I don't quite know whether to go back and hit him, or — what's that? — get down here on my knees and pray for him? Yes, that was the thought coming up in me; but it would be the first time I ever really did pray. It's queer; very queer; and he's queer too; aye, take him fore and aft, he's about the queerest old man Stubb ever sailed with. How he flashed at me! — his eyes like powder-pans! Is he mad? Anyway, there's something on his mind, as sure as there must be something on a deck when it cracks. He isn't in his bed now, either, more than three hours out of the twenty-four; and he doesn't sleep then. Didn't that Dough-Boy, the steward, tell me that in the morning he always finds the old man's hammock clothes all rumpled and tumbled, and the sheets down at the foot, and the coverlet almost tied into knots, and the pillow a sort of frightful hot, as though a baked brick had been on it? A hot old man! I guess he's got what some folks ashore call a conscience; it's a kind of Tic-Dolly-row, they say — worse than a toothache. Well, well; I don't know what it is, but the Lord keep me from catching it. He's full of riddles; I wonder what he goes into the after hold for every night, as Dough-Boy tells me he suspects; what's that for, I'd like to know? Who's made appointments with him in the hold? Isn't that queer, now? But there's no telling; it's the old game. Here goes for a snooze. Damn me, it's worth a fellow's while to be born into the world, if only to fall right asleep. And now that I think of it, that's about the first thing babies do, and that's sort of queer, too. Damn me, but all things are queer, come to think of them. But that's against my principles. Think not, is my eleventh commandment; and sleep when you can, is my twelfth. So here goes again. But how's that? Didn't he call me a dog? Blazes! He called me ten times a donkey, and piled a lot of jackasses on top of that! He might as well have kicked me, and been done with it. Maybe he did kick me, and I didn't notice it, I was so taken aback by his brow, somehow. It flashed like a bleached bone. What the devil's the matter with me? I don't stand right on my legs. Running afoul of that old man has sort of turned me inside out. By the Lord, I must have been dreaming, though — how? how? how? — but the only way is to stow it; so here goes to the hammock again; and in the morning I'll see how this plaguey hocus-pocus looks when I think it over by daylight."
